You have to decide which of the given inferences, if any, follow from the given statement. Statement: In a cricket match between Team-A and Team-B, the total number of runs scored by Team-B were 240, out of which 90 runs were scored by a single batsman. Inferences: I. The batsman was highly skilled and performed exceptionally well. II. 37.5% of the players in Team-B scored runs in that match.
questions.questionHtml:
Directions: A statement is given followed by two inferences I and II. You have to consider the statement to be true even if it seems to be at variance with commonly known facts. You have to decide which of the given inferences, if any, follow from the given statement.
Statement:
In a cricket match between Team-A and Team-B, the total number of runs scored by Team-B were 240, out of which 90 runs were scored by a single batsman.
Inferences:
I. The batsman was highly skilled and performed exceptionally well.
II. 37.5% of the players in Team-B scored runs in that match.

options.text: If both I and II follow
If neither I nor II follows

questions.solution:
Check each inference

Inference I: “The batsman was highly skilled and performed exceptionally well.”

The statement only gives numbers: 240 total runs and 90 by one batsman.
From this, skill or “exceptional” performance is a value judgment, not a logical necessity; the 90 could be due to weak bowling, small ground, or many overs faced.
So, Inference I does not follow.

Inference II: “37.5% of the players in Team-B scored runs in that match.”

Nothing in the statement tells how many players actually scored runs (maybe all 11, maybe some got out on 0, maybe some did not bat at all).
The statement has no information about the count of run-scoring players or team size, so “37.5%” is completely unsupported.
So, Inference II does not follow.

Conclusion: Neither I nor II follows from the given statement.

questions.question: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow. The distinction between "High" and "Low" art is a construct that has vexed cultural theorists for centuries. "High" art, often associated with classical music, opera, and canonical literature, is frequently lauded for its intellectual profundity, complexity, and its capacity to transcend the immediate context. It is perceived as timeless, demanding of its audience a certain level of cultural capital and education to be fully appreciated. Conversely, "Low" art, or popular culture (pop music, blockbuster films, genre fiction), is often dismissed as commercial, simplistic, and ephemeral—a mere distraction for the masses rather than a source of genuine aesthetic or intellectual engagement. This binary, however, is deeply problematic. It is often rooted not in objective aesthetic merit but in social stratification. The gatekeepers of "High" art have historically been the socioeconomic elite, who use their control over cultural institutions (museums, universities, opera houses) to legitimize their own tastes as inherently superior, thereby reinforcing their social standing. Pierre Bourdieu's concept of "cultural capital" precisely delineates this phenomenon, where familiarity with "High" art functions as a marker of social distinction. Furthermore, this distinction often ignores the formal complexity and thematic depth present in so-called "Low" art. The intricate narrative structures of modern television series or the sophisticated lyrical and rhythmic innovations in hip-hop often rival the complexity of forms traditionally deemed "High." The line is not only blurry; it is, in many respects, arbitrary and self-serving. Q- What is the central thesis of the passage?
